title: Fisher exact test
biology: Survival of rare resistant and susceptible clones
design: Two small independent clone groups; binary survival after exposure.
data_characteristics: Two categorical variables in a 2 × 2 table
Small counts, including possibly empty cells
The target is an association, expressed as an odds ratio
question: Are survival odds associated with clone type?
null: The population odds ratio for clone type and survival is 1.
options: Check the row and column order before interpreting the odds ratio.
alternative = "two.sided" tests association in either direction.
The confidence interval is for the odds ratio.
assumptions: Each clone contributes one independent observation.
Outcomes belong to exactly one table cell.
Use an appropriate paired analysis for matched clones.
parametric: Logistic regression can add predictors; sparse-data methods may be needed.
More observations improve precision when the interval is wide.
nonparametric: Fisher’s test already provides exact conditional inference.
Use an exact paired test for discordant matched pairs.

plot_args.note: Show each group’s two outcome counts.
Link outcome colors to the legend.
Put small counts directly on the bars.
Leave label space above the bars.

code_simulate:
set.seed(3106)
d <- data.frame(clone = 1:24,
  type = rep(c("Susceptible", "Resistant"), each = 12))
d$survived <- rbinom(24, 1, rep(c(.20, .65), each = 12))
write.csv(d, file.path(out_dir, "data.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
code_plot:
par(mar = c(4, 5, 2, 1), las = 1)
bars <- barplot(t(tab), beside = TRUE, border = NA,
  col = c("#d5d5d5", "#126887"), ylim = c(0, max(tab) + 3),
  names.arg = rownames(tab), ylab = "Clones")
text(bars, t(tab), labels = c(t(tab)), pos = 3)
legend("topright", c("Died", "Survived"),
       fill = c("#d5d5d5", "#126887"), bty = "n")
code_analysis:
tab <- table(factor(d$type, levels = c("Susceptible", "Resistant")),
             factor(d$survived, levels = c(0, 1)))
fit <- fisher.test(tab, alternative = "two.sided")
odds_ratio <- unname(fit$estimate)
ci <- fit$conf.int
practice: Why is an odds ratio of 3 not the same as a threefold survival probability?
generating_model: Generate 12 independent susceptible clones with survival probability 0.20 and 12 independent resistant clones with probability 0.65. Each contributes one Bernoulli outcome; small table cells are intentional.
generating_truth: The resistant-to-susceptible population survival odds ratio is (0.65/0.35)/(0.20/0.80), approximately 7.43. The odds-ratio-one null is false.
teaching_point: Exact inference handles sparse counts, but it cannot create the precision missing from a small sample.
